title: Nature loves change
hookLine: nothing is more natural than change, Marcus writes (Meditations 4.36)

cards: Find an old photo of yourself. Ten years old, maybe, squinting at the camera. The haircut is gone, the house may be gone, the people holding the camera may be gone.
Still, when a gray hair shows up, a favorite café closes, or a friend moves across the country, something in us says: this isn't supposed to happen. It's easy to treat change like a malfunction.
Marcus Aurelius wrote himself a note about exactly that.

teach.b: Marcus was a Roman emperor who wrote his private notes in Greek. The book's own headings place parts of it in army camps. They're known as the Meditations.
In Book Four he tells himself to keep watching how everything comes about through change, then adds a surprising line.

teach.h: IT LOVES NOTHING SO MUCH AS TO CHANGE.
teach.b: In George Long's old translation, the nature of the universe "loves nothing so much as to change the things which are and to make new things like them." Notice the word loves. Not puts up with, not suffers.
Change is what nature most enjoys doing. The things that exist now, he goes on, are seeds of what will come from them.
Elsewhere Marcus quotes Heraclitus, the older Greek thinker remembered for saying that everything flows. And in Book Seven he makes it ordinary. Are you afraid of change?

teach.h: THE BATH NEEDS THE WOOD TO BURN.
teach.b: You can't take a warm bath unless the wood changes in the fire. You can't eat unless the food changes in you. The very things that keep you alive are changes.

So Marcus isn't asking himself to like every loss. He's asking something smaller and harder: to stop treating change as an insult, as if the universe had broken its promise. It never promised to stay still.

how: Readers of the Stoics often keep a short line like this one in view, and some make a habit of pausing to notice change in small things, such as the breath or the light, as Marcus advised himself.

games.why: in Book Seven he asks who is afraid of change, and points out that even a bath needs the wood to change in the fire.

practice: Pick something small and close: your breath going in and out, the light on the wall, a sound that rises and fades, the warmth of your hands. Just watch it change, without fixing it or holding it.
If a bigger change in your life comes to mind, let it sit beside the small one for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Heraclitus, the older Greek thinker Marcus echoes, remembered for saying that everything flows, nothing stays the same. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, the language Marcus wrote in: change, a turning into something else. the Stoics used it for the constant change of nature.

carryVoice: Your line: change is natural. What exists now is the seed of what comes next. Day one hundred eighty-eight, done.
